Authentication code flow

Source: vignettes/authentication.Rmd
authentication.Rmd

This document serves as a walkthrough of how otndata’s authentication framework is set up. I welcome contributions, but I worry that this flow is a bit opaque and might trip someone up right out of the gate. As such, it is mainly geared toward those who wish to contribute to, or develop with, otndata. This package is intended to interface with the Plone API, so what’s written here will be a mix of things you can find in that documentation and otndata’s wrapper on top of that.

Authentication code flow

In order to log in, we must POST our username and password to the Plone CMS REST API. To get and access user credentials, a lot of inspiration (and code!) has been taken from the tidycensus package, which writes credentials to the user’s .Renviron file for use across sessions. The upside to this method is that it is easy to code in base R; the downside is that secrets are stored in plain text on the user’s machine. This is universally considered unacceptable, but I’ve decided that interacting with telemetry data low-stakes enough to take the risk.

To allow users to store credentials for multiple networks, credentials are written to OTN_PASS.{network} and OTN_USER.{network} environmental variables. Again, these are stored in plain text in the users .Renviron file if the user wishes to use them across sessions. When an R session is started, the .Renviron file is loaded along with other system variables, meaning the credentials can be accessed via Sys.getenv("OTN_USER.{network}") or Sys.getenv("OTN_PASS.{network}").

The “global environment”

“Setting” credentials takes a lot of inspiration from ggplot2::set_theme, which uses a “ggplot_global” environment to hold user-set options for ggplot2:

Environment that holds various global variables and settings for ggplot, such as the current theme. It is not exported and should not be directly manipulated by other packages. ggplot_global <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())

Mirroring this, we have an otn_global envrionment. You can see what’s inside of it like so:

library(otndata)

# Note the 3 colons
ls(otndata:::otn_global)
#> [1] "act"       "otn_devel"

If you use devtools::load_all(), you can interact with it like you would an R list.

otn_global[["fake_info"]] <- 1234

ls(otn_global)
#> [1] "fake_info"
otn_global$fake_info
#> [1] 1234

It is in this way that we manage our credentials within the R session.

Logging in

When the user runs otn_login("{network}"), we first use network to figure out what the URL of the specific Plone instance is. This URL is placed into the otn_global environment under otn_global${network}$server_url. We can now think of otn_global${network} as a list that will hold information about the server, including our to-be-found session token.

Next, otndata looks for the OTN_USER.{network} and OTN_PASS.{network} environment variables and runs a temporary version of otn_set_credentials if they aren’t found. If they aren’t found, this places your credentials in your current R session’s environment in plain text such that these will be wiped when you close or restart R.

Finally, we POST our username (as “login”) and password (as “password”) to the Plone CMS using the credentials we’ve grabbed and server URL we’ve sussed out. If the login is successful an authorization token is returned that we must attach to all requests that need the user to be logged in. otndata places this token in the otn_global environment under its respective network. We wind up with something that looks like this, assuming you’ve just logged into the ACT Network’s data portal:

#> ✔ Login successful!
ls(otndata:::otn_global)
#> [1] "act"       "otn_devel"

otndata:::otn_global$act
#> $server_url
#> [1] "https://data.theactnetwork.com"
#> 
#> $token
#> [1] "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJvYnJpZW4iLCJleHAiOjE3OTIyMDQ3NTUsImZ1bGxuYW1lIjoiTWlrZSBPJ0JyaWVuIn0.ZndqyvzxtJO-pH20HOHxKMOdu-mX8v-i5zfXs2aXxGQ"

Multiple Networks

Setting thing up in this way allows us to:

  • Shield critical information from most actions of the user, but allow them to change things if they know what they’re doing
  • Repeatedly use the same token
  • Log into multiple networks

As server information and the authentication token are stored under the network, we can log into multiple networks in the same session and extract the token via otn_global[["{network}"]]$token. Note that while I’m using otndata::: here, you do not need to do this in the code or while developing.

otn_login("otn_devel")
#> ✔ Login successful!

ls(otndata:::otn_global)
#> [1] "act"       "otn_devel"
otndata:::otn_global$otn_devel
#> $server_url
#> [1] "https://members.devel.oceantrack.org"
#> 
#> $token
#> [1] "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJtb2JyaWVuIiwiZXhwIjoxNzkyMjA0NzU1LCJmdWxsbmFtZSI6Ik1pa2UgTydCcmllbiJ9.Kll_dgk_zsWfDa28IquaZvGca2ojlkDIwnNnan2zr2E"
otndata:::otn_global[["otn_devel"]]$token
#> [1] "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJtb2JyaWVuIiwiZXhwIjoxNzkyMjA0NzU1LCJmdWxsbmFtZSI6Ik1pa2UgTydCcmllbiJ9.Kll_dgk_zsWfDa28IquaZvGca2ojlkDIwnNnan2zr2E"
